title: Pass a booking on, and the right to work rules can now treat you as the employer
seo_title: Right to work checks now cover sub-contractors
dek: Since 1 October, the UK's illegal working rules reach individual sub-contractors and people on worker's contracts. Anyone contracted to provide work who passes it on can be treated as employing whoever actually turns up. What that means for crew bookings.
summary: Since 1 October 2026, UK right to work checks cover worker's contracts and individual sub-contractors, and liability can run up a contract chain.
body:
Since 1 October, the UK's illegal working rules no longer stop at the payroll. [Section 48](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2025/31/section/48) of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025, switched on that day by [S.I. 2026/683](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/683), inserts new sections 14A and 15A into the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006. For sections 15 to 24 of that Act, "employing" someone now includes engaging an individual under a worker's contract, or engaging them as an individual sub-contractor. Online matching services are in as well: providing the details of an individual service provider to potential clients or customers counts.

The explanatory note to the commencement regulations says as much: the change extends the illegal working provisions in sections 15 to 24 to arrangements beyond contracts of employment.

Then there is section 15A, which is the bit that should make production offices sit up. Where a person is contracted to provide work and enters a contract under which someone else does it, that person is treated as employing any individual who personally provides the work. That holds where it has no contract with the individual, and where it does not even know they are the one doing it. And it applies "regardless of whether that contract is the first or any other contract in a chain of contracts".

## What that looks like on a job

Events run on chains. A client hires an agency, the agency hires a production company, the production company hires an AV supplier, and the AV supplier rings a crew chief, who rings the people they trust.

Section 14A(3) defines an individual sub-contractor as an individual who has a contract with person B to provide work or services, where person B has contracted with a third party and the individual has not. Hold that up against a typical crew booking and it describes a lot of us.

Section 15A is the one that runs uphill. Anyone in that chain who was contracted to deliver the work and passed it on can be treated as employing the person who actually turns up with the cable reel. On our reading, that includes the crew chief who took a booking for four and filled three of the slots with mates. If that is you, you are not just the freelancer in this story. For these purposes you are the employer as well.

Our reading of the client end: section 15A only bites on someone who is themselves contracted to provide the work and contracts it onward. A corporate client buying a finished event is not obviously in that position. A client that engages an individual directly on a worker's contract is a different matter, because section 14A(1)(a) covers exactly that.

## What the Home Office expects

The Home Office updated its [employer's guide](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/right-to-work-checks-employers-guide) and its [right to work checklist](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/right-to-work-checklist/employers-right-to-work-checklist-accessible-version) on 1 October. The checklist says a prescribed right to work check must be carried out before the worker starts, for a worker engaged under a worker's contract and for one engaged as an individual sub-contractor.

It also asks a question every freelancer will recognise: "Does the contractual arrangement permit substitution?" Where it does, the checklist's answer is: "Any substitute undergoes a prescribed right to work check before starting work or providing services." The old habit of sending a mate when you have double-booked now comes with paperwork attached.

Substitution is not a trigger in sections 14A or 15A, as we read them. It turns up in the checklist as a screening question, and as part of the defence. That defence, the statutory excuse against extended liability, has three parts in the checklist: a written statement containing the prescribed contractual terms and conditions, substitution controls where they apply, and identity verification.

## The penalty, and the code

On penalties, the roofing trade body [NFRC](https://www.nfrc.co.uk/resource/right-to-work-checks.html) put it like this on 9 October: "A business may face a civil penalty of up to £60,000 for each illegal worker." That is a maximum, stated by a trade body. The Home Office's [code of practice](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/illegal-working-penalties-codes-of-practice-for-employers), now dated 1 October 2026 with "draft" removed from its title, covers the factors the Home Office takes into account when it sets the amount of a penalty. We could not read the code's own figures for this piece. Be wary of anyone quoting precise starting points at you without a page number.

## Our view

It is tempting to read all this as IR35 by the back door. [Roots Contractor Insurance](https://rootsinsurance.co.uk/right-to-work-checks-contractors-october-2026/), a contractor insurance broker, argues it is not: in its view the change does not turn every limited company contractor into an employee, and right to work sits apart from IR35. We agree. As we read them, the new sections are about who has to check, not about anyone's employment status.

Roots also expects identity and right to work compliance to become a more visible part of onboarding. Our own guess is that share code requests start arriving with booking confirmations, and that crew terms grow a clause about substitutes and onward subcontracting.

NFRC tells its members to review their existing arrangements rather than assume their current checks and contracts are sufficient, and expects the risk to be greatest for those with more complex labour arrangements. An event supply chain four or five contracts deep, with a crew chief's group chat at the bottom of it, is about as complex as they come.

confirmed.text: Section 48 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 inserts new sections 14A and 15A into the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006.

Under new section 14A(1), a reference to employing someone in sections 15 to 24 includes engaging an individual under a worker's contract, engaging an individual sub-contractor, and an online matching service providing the details of an individual service provider to potential clients or customers.

Section 14A(3) defines an individual sub-contractor as an individual who has a contract with person B to provide work or services, where person B has contracted with a third party and the individual has not.

Under new section 15A, a person contracted to provide work who enters a contract under which another person does it is treated as employing any individual who personally provides the work, even with no contract with them or no knowledge that they are doing it, at any point in a chain of contracts.
S.I. 2026/683, made on 24 June 2026, brings section 48 into force on 1 October 2026.
The explanatory note to S.I. 2026/683 says section 48 extends the illegal working provisions in sections 15 to 24 of the 2006 Act to arrangements beyond contracts of employment.
The Home Office employer's guide to right to work checks was last updated on 1 October 2026, with final employer guidance added for that date.
The Home Office checklist says a prescribed right to work check must be carried out before the worker starts for a worker's contract and for an individual sub-contractor.
The checklist asks whether the contractual arrangement permits substitution, and where it does, expects any substitute to undergo a prescribed right to work check before starting.

The checklist lists three parts of the statutory excuse against extended liability: a written statement with the prescribed contractual terms, substitution controls where applicable, and identity verification.
The code of practice is listed on GOV.UK as dated 1 October 2026, with 'draft' removed from its title, and covers the factors the Home Office takes into account when setting the amount of a penalty.
The trade body NFRC says a business may face a civil penalty of up to £60,000 for each illegal worker.

impact:
**Freelance crew.** The check has to happen before you start, so expect it before your first day on a new booking rather than on the morning of the show. If you hold an eVisa, the Home Office checklist says the online service must be used, with a share code and your date of birth, so know how to generate one. The other routes are a manual document check or a check by a registered digital verification service provider. A clipped passport is not acceptable proof.

**Sending a substitute.** If your terms allow it, the substitute needs a prescribed check before they start. Tell the booker days ahead, not from the car park.

**Crew chiefs who book their own team.** If you take a booking and hand parts of it to others, section 15A can treat you as employing whoever personally does the work. Check them before they start and keep the record. Put the terms in writing too.

**Production companies and AV suppliers (and the agencies above them).** Map your chains, job by job. Where workers come to you through another employer or a matching platform, the Home Office expects a written statement with the prescribed contract terms to be in place before work starts. On the day, identity verification has to confirm that "the individual carrying out the work or services is the same individual" who was checked. In our view that makes it a job for whoever runs sign-in at crew call.

**Records.** Keep copies "for the duration of employment and for 2 years afterwards", and record the date the check was made. The Home Office is blunt about it: "Simply writing a date on the copy document on its own will not be sufficient."

**Before you redraft any contract,** read the code of practice and the full employer's guide. The checklist only says the written statement must contain "the prescribed contractual terms and conditions"; it does not list them.
verdict_note: In force since 1 October. If you book people who book people, get the check and the substitute rule in place before the next job, with paperwork to prove both. Read the code of practice before you rewrite a single clause.
